title: Epidemiology: Measures and Study Design
subtitle: Incidence, prevalence, morbidity, mortality and the types of epidemiological study
subject: Biology
syllabusDotPoints: analyse patterns of non-infectious diseases in populations, including their incidence and prevalence, including but not limited to: nutritional diseases, diseases caused by environmental exposure
evaluate the method used in an example of an epidemiological study
Distinguish between incidence, prevalence, morbidity and mortality as used in epidemiological studies
Compare the features of observational, analytical and experimental epidemiological studies
Discuss the features of randomised clinical trials, cross-sectional studies, case studies and cohort studies
Assess approaches taken to reduce selection error and confounding factors in an epidemiological study
lessonIntent: Students can distinguish and calculate incidence, prevalence, morbidity and mortality, compare observational, analytical and experimental study designs, and judge whether epidemiological data supports a causal or merely correlational conclusion.
examSkill: Read an epidemiological data table, distinguish total counts from age-standardised rates, and evaluate whether the evidence supports causation rather than just correlation.

introVoiceover.text: Welcome to HSC Science. This is HSC Biology. Today: measuring disease and reading study designs. Let's get into it.

scenes.heading: Proving smoking kills, without an experiment
scenes.body: Doll and Hill linked smoking to lung cancer with data from populations, not experiments. The tobacco industry called it just a correlation.
scenes.callout: How do you prove cause when you can't run the experiment?
scenes.caption: Doll and Hill's British Doctors Study showed heavy smokers died of lung cancer at many times the rate of non-smokers.

voiceover.text: So, in 1950, Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill compared people with lung cancer against people without it, and found the cancer patients were far more likely to be smokers. The tobacco industry pounced, arguing it was only a correlation. So Doll and Hill did something clever. From 1951 they followed around forty thousand British doctors for decades, recording who smoked and what each of them eventually died of. Heavy smokers died of lung cancer at many times the rate of non smokers, and the more they smoked, the higher that rate climbed. That way of thinking is epidemiology, and by the end of today you'll be able to measure disease in a population and judge what the numbers actually prove.

scenes.heading: Four ways to measure a disease
scenes.body: Incidence, prevalence, morbidity and mortality each answer a different question about disease in a population.

bullets.text: Incidence: how many NEW cases appear per population per time period.
Prevalence: how many EXISTING cases there are at one point in time.
Morbidity: how much illness a disease causes, e.g. hospital admissions.
Mortality: how many deaths from the disease per population per year.

scenes.secondary: Prevalence is roughly incidence multiplied by how long people live with the disease, so a chronic disease like Type 2 diabetes can have modest incidence but high prevalence.
scenes.callout: New cases, existing cases, illness, deaths. Four different numbers.
scenes.caption: Incidence = new cases, prevalence = existing cases, morbidity = illness, mortality = deaths.

voiceover.text: OK, before you can prove anything, you have to measure the disease properly, and there are four measures, each answering a different question. Incidence counts new cases in a population over a set time, so it tells you how fast a disease is appearing. Eighteen hundred new melanoma diagnoses in ten million people in one year is an incidence of eighteen per hundred thousand per year. Prevalence counts all existing cases at one moment, old and new, so it tells you how much disease is in the community right now. Morbidity is about illness rather than death. It describes how much sickness a disease causes, often measured as the rate of people unwell with it, or as hospital admissions. And mortality is the number of deaths from the disease per population per year. Here's the link worth remembering. Prevalence is roughly incidence times the average duration, so a lifelong disease like Type 2 diabetes builds up a high prevalence even when its incidence is modest.

scenes.heading: The words you need
scenes.body: Three more terms run through every epidemiology question.

bullets.text: Epidemiology: the study of how disease is distributed in populations and what drives it.
Confounding variable: a third factor linked to both the exposure and the outcome.
Age-standardised rate: a rate adjusted for age structure so populations compare fairly.

scenes.callout: Epidemiology guides public health; confounders and age can both mislead.
scenes.caption: Epidemiology, confounding variable, age-standardised rate.

voiceover.text: Let's pin down three more terms you'll use all lesson. Epidemiology is the study of how disease is distributed across populations and what drives it, and public health agencies use it to decide where to aim prevention, screening and treatment. A confounding variable is a third factor linked to both the exposure you're studying and the disease, and it can fake a relationship that isn't really there. And an age standardised rate has been adjusted for a population's age structure, so two populations with different age profiles can be compared fairly.

scenes.heading: Observational, analytical and experimental studies
scenes.body: Epidemiological studies fall into three groups, trading off speed, cost and how strongly they can show cause.

bullets.text: Observational: describe without intervening, e.g. case studies and cross-sectional studies.
Analytical: compare groups to test a link, e.g. cohort and case-control studies.
Experimental: the researcher intervenes, e.g. the randomised controlled trial.

scenes.secondary: Randomisation spreads confounders evenly between groups, which is why the RCT is the strongest evidence for cause. But you can't ethically assign people to a harmful exposure, so risk questions usually need observational or analytical designs.
scenes.caption: Observational (case study, cross-sectional), analytical (cohort, case-control) and experimental (RCT) studies.

voiceover.text: Now, how do you actually generate the data? Epidemiological studies fall into three broad groups. Observational studies watch and describe without intervening. A case study describes one patient, or a small cluster, in detail, and it's often how a new disease is first noticed. A cross sectional study is a snapshot, measuring exposure and disease across a population at one moment, which is great for prevalence but can't tell you which came first. Analytical studies are still observational, but they compare groups to test a hypothesis. A cohort study follows disease free people forward in time, comparing the exposed with the unexposed, so it shows the exposure came first, which is exactly what the doctors study did. A case control study works backwards from people who already have the disease, which suits rare diseases but relies on memory. Experimental studies are where the researcher intervenes, and the classic one is the randomised controlled trial, which randomly assigns people to a treatment or a placebo. Randomisation spreads confounders evenly, so it's the strongest evidence for cause. The catch is ethics, because you can't assign people to smoke for twenty years.

rows: Compares groups to test a link

scenes.heading: Why correlation isn't causation
scenes.body: A confounding variable links to both the exposure and the outcome, so it can manufacture an association that looks causal but isn't.

bullets.text: A confounder is tied to both the exposure being studied and the disease.
Classic case: coffee looked linked to lung cancer, but coffee drinkers also smoked.
Reduce confounding by matching, statistical adjustment or randomisation.
Reduce selection error with random, representative, large samples.

scenes.secondary: To call something causal, look for strength, consistency across studies, a dose-response relationship and biological plausibility.
scenes.callout: Find the hidden third factor before you believe the link.
scenes.caption: A confounder linked to both exposure and outcome can fake a causal link; control it and selection error before concluding cause.

voiceover.text: Here's the idea the whole topic turns on. Two things can be correlated without one causing the other, and the usual culprit is a confounding variable. The classic example, early studies found coffee drinking was associated with lung cancer. But back then, coffee drinkers were also far more likely to smoke. Smoking is the confounder, linked to coffee drinking and genuinely causing lung cancer, and once you control for it, the coffee link basically vanishes. So how do you reduce confounding? Match cases and controls on that factor, adjust for it statistically, or best of all, randomise. Selection error matters too. If your sample isn't representative of the population, the result won't apply to everyone, so good studies use large, randomly chosen samples. To finally claim cause, you look for a bundle of signs, a strong effect, the same result across many studies, a dose response where more exposure means more disease, and a believable biological mechanism. That bundle is how smoking was proven to cause lung cancer.

scenes.heading: Reading a data table
scenes.question: Illustrative Type 2 diabetes data for Australia: in 2000, 640,000 cases in 19.2 million people; in 2022, 1,300,000 cases in 25.9 million. Crude prevalence rose 3.3% to 5.0%, but age-standardised prevalence went 4.1% to 4.2%. Is the diabetes epidemic genuinely worsening?
scenes.coachNote: Separate total cases from rates, and crude rates from age-standardised rates, before you judge the trend.
steps: Total cases roughly doubled, but the population also grew by about a third (19.2 to 25.9 million), so raw counts overstate the trend.
Crude prevalence rose from 3.3% to 5.0%, yet this partly reflects an ageing population, since older people have higher diabetes rates.
Age-standardised prevalence barely moved, 4.1% to 4.2%, which removes the age effect.
So the underlying rate in comparable age groups is roughly stable; most of the rise is demographic change.
Answer: the apparent worsening is largely population growth and ageing, not a surging underlying rate ✓
scenes.caption: Age-standardised prevalence (4.1% to 4.2%) shows the underlying T2D rate is roughly stable despite rising totals.

voiceover.text: Let's read a data table, because this is exactly what the exam asks. Here's some illustrative Type 2 diabetes data for Australia. In the year two thousand, six hundred and forty thousand cases in nineteen point two million people. By twenty twenty two, one point three million cases in twenty five point nine million people. Is the epidemic genuinely worsening? First, total cases roughly doubled, but the population grew by about a third, so raw counts are inflated just by there being more people. Second, crude prevalence rose from three point three to five percent, but that partly reflects an ageing population, because older people have higher diabetes rates. Third, and this is the decisive number, age standardised prevalence barely moved, from four point one to four point two percent. So in comparable age groups the underlying rate is essentially stable, and most of the apparent surge is population growth and ageing.

scenes.heading: Calculating the measures
scenes.question: In a population of 5 million, 450 new cases of bowel cancer are diagnosed in one year, 8,500 people are living with it, and 90 people die of it during the year. Find (a) incidence per 100,000 per year, (b) prevalence as a percentage, (c) mortality rate per 100,000 per year.
scenes.coachNote: All three measures use the whole population as the denominator; what changes is the numerator.
steps: (a) Incidence = new cases ÷ population × 100,000 = 450 ÷ 5,000,000 × 100,000 = 9 per 100,000 per year.
(c) Mortality = deaths ÷ population × 100,000 = 90 ÷ 5,000,000 × 100,000 = 1.8 per 100,000 per year.
Trap: dividing deaths by the 8,500 people with the disease gives a case fatality (about 1%), not a mortality rate.
scenes.caption: Incidence 9 per 100,000/yr, prevalence 0.17%, mortality 1.8 per 100,000/yr.

voiceover.text: Now let's crunch the numbers, because these calculations come up directly. A population of five million. In one year, four hundred and fifty new bowel cancer cases, eight and a half thousand people living with the disease, and ninety deaths from it. Part a, incidence is new cases over the population, times a hundred thousand, so four hundred and fifty divided by five million, times a hundred thousand, gives nine per hundred thousand per year. Part b, prevalence is existing cases over the population, times a hundred, so eight and a half thousand divided by five million is zero point one seven percent. Part c, mortality is deaths over the population, so ninety divided by five million, times a hundred thousand, is one point eight per hundred thousand per year. Watch the trap here. If you divide the deaths by the people who have the disease, you get a case fatality of about one percent, which is a different measure entirely.

scenes.heading: Three traps
scenes.body: Trap 1: treating prevalence and incidence as the same thing. Incidence is new cases over time; prevalence is all existing cases at a moment.
scenes.secondary: Trap 2: reading correlation as causation, when a confounder may explain the whole association. Trap 3: assuming a rising rate means the disease is genuinely getting more common, when population growth, ageing, or better screening can all lift the numbers. Always check whether a rate is crude or age-standardised.
scenes.callout: New is not total, linked is not caused, rising is not always real.
scenes.caption: Incidence is not prevalence; correlation is not causation; a rising count is not always a rising rate.

voiceover.text: Three traps that quietly cost marks every year. Trap one, the big one, treating incidence and prevalence as the same thing. Incidence is the rate of new cases over time, while prevalence is all existing cases at a moment, and they can move in opposite directions, so always say which one you mean. Trap two, reading correlation as causation. A statistical link doesn't prove cause, because a confounder might explain the whole thing, so you need that bundle of causal criteria first. Trap three, assuming a rising rate means the disease is genuinely getting more common. Rates can climb just from population growth, from an ageing population, or from better screening picking up cases that were always there. So before you interpret any trend, check whether the rate is crude or age standardised.

scenes.heading: Quick check
scenes.question: In high-income countries, the prevalence of HIV has risen over the last two decades, yet the incidence of HIV has fallen. Explain how both can be true at the same time.
answerSteps: Incidence counts new infections per year, while prevalence counts everyone currently living with HIV.
Prevalence is roughly incidence multiplied by the average duration of the disease.
Antiretroviral therapy keeps people alive far longer, so the average duration rises sharply.
Even with fewer new infections each year, people stay in the existing-cases pool for much longer, so that pool grows.
Answer: falling incidence with longer survival raises duration, so prevalence climbs ✓
scenes.caption: Longer survival raises duration, so prevalence rises even as incidence (new infections) falls.

voiceover.text: Quick check, and this one separates the students who really get incidence and prevalence. In high income countries, the prevalence of H I V has risen over the last twenty years, yet the incidence of H I V has fallen. How can both be true at once? Pause and reason it through. Okay, let's build it. Incidence counts new infections each year, while prevalence counts everyone currently living with the disease. Recall the link, prevalence is roughly incidence times the average duration. Antiretroviral therapy keeps people alive for decades, so the average duration shoots up. So even though fewer people are newly infected each year, those already infected stay in the pool of existing cases far longer, and that pool keeps growing. Falling incidence, longer survival, rising prevalence, all perfectly consistent.

scenes.heading: Lock it in
points: Incidence is new cases over time; prevalence is all existing cases at a point; morbidity is illness; mortality is deaths.
Prevalence is roughly incidence times duration, so chronic disease builds high prevalence.
Observational studies describe, analytical studies compare groups, experimental studies (RCTs) intervene.
Confounders and selection error can fake causation, so control them before concluding cause.
Always check whether a rate is crude or age-standardised before judging a trend.
scenes.finalPrompt: Given epidemiological data? Ask: is this a count or a rate, crude or age-standardised, correlation or proven cause?
scenes.caption: Five takeaways: the four measures, the duration link, the three study types, confounding, and crude vs standardised.

voiceover.text: Let's lock it in. First, incidence is new cases over time, prevalence is all existing cases at a point in time, morbidity is illness, and mortality is deaths. Second, prevalence is roughly incidence times duration, which is why a chronic disease builds up a high prevalence. Third, observational studies like case studies and cross sectional surveys describe, analytical studies like cohort and case control studies compare groups, and experimental studies like the randomised controlled trial intervene. Fourth, confounding variables and selection error can fake causation, so you have to control them before you trust a link. And fifth, always check whether a rate is crude or age standardised before you read anything into a trend. Whenever you're handed epidemiological data, ask whether it's a count or a rate, crude or standardised, and correlation or proven cause. See you next lesson.
